Interlude: The Mars Climate Orbiter — $327M Lost in Translation

Delivered between Module 2 (Technical Writing Fundamentals) and Module 3 (Design Documents & RFCs)

---

September 23, 1999. ‍​A Thursday.

‍​At the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, a room full of engineers stared at their screens and waited. ​​Nine and a half months of waiting was almost over. ​​The Mars Climate Orbiter — a spacecraft roughly the size of a small car, carrying instruments designed to study the Martian atmosphere — was about to execute the most critical maneuver of its mission: Mars Orbit Insertion.

​​The plan was precise. ​​The spacecraft would fire its main engine for sixteen minutes, slow down, and slip into orbit around Mars. ​​It would pass behind the planet, out of radio contact for about twenty minutes, and then re-emerge on the other side, captured by Martian gravity. ‌​Ground controllers had rehearsed the sequence dozens of times. ‌​They had sent the commands. ‌​Everything was nominal.

‌​The spacecraft passed behind Mars at 09:04 UTC. ‌​Contact was lost, as expected.

‌‌Twenty minutes passed. ‌​Then thirty. ‌​Then an hour.

‌​It never came back.

​​---

What Went Wrong

The investigation took weeks. ​​Hundreds of engineers from NASA and Lockheed Martin — the contractor that built the spacecraft — pored over telemetry data, software logs, and mission records. ‌​When they found the answer, it was so simple that several people initially refused to believe it.

​​The spacecraft's thruster software, written by Lockheed Martin, calculated impulse in pound-force seconds — an imperial unit. ​​NASA's navigation team at JPL, who used the thruster data to plan trajectory corrections, expected the data in newton-seconds — the metric equivalent. ‌​One pound-force second equals approximately 4.45 newton-seconds. ‌​The software interface specification said "total impulse." ​​It did not specify which unit system.

​​Both teams were competent. ‌​Both teams were experienced. ‌‌Both teams assumed the other was using their standard. ​‌Neither team checked. ‌​Neither team asked.

​​The error was tiny on any single maneuver — a small percentage off. ‌‌But the Mars Climate Orbiter performed dozens of trajectory correction maneuvers over its nine-month journey. ‌‌Each one was slightly wrong in the same direction. ​​The errors accumulated silently, invisibly, for 416 million miles.

​​By the time the spacecraft reached Mars, it was 170 kilometers lower than planned. ‌‌Instead of passing safely above the atmosphere at 226 kilometers altitude, it entered at roughly 57 kilometers. ​‌At that altitude, the atmosphere is thick enough to matter. ‌‌The spacecraft either burned up from friction or skipped off the atmosphere and tumbled into solar orbit, forever lost.

‌​$327 million. ‌‌Nine and a half months. ‌‌Thousands of hours of engineering work. ​​Destroyed by an ambiguity in a specification document.

‌​---

The Specification

Here is the haunting part. ‌​The interface specification existed. ‌​There was a document that described the data format exchanged between Lockheed Martin's thruster software and JPL's navigation system. ​​The document listed the data fields. ​​It described the calculation. ‌​It said "total impulse."

​​It did not say "in newton-seconds" or "in pound-force seconds."

​​Someone writing the spec thought the unit was obvious. ‌​Maybe they assumed everyone used metric. ‌​Maybe they assumed the SI unit was implied. ‌‌Maybe they were in a hurry and skipped what felt like a trivial detail. ​​We will never know who wrote that line, or what they were thinking when they left the unit off.

​​What we know is this: the information needed to prevent the disaster was a four-word addition to a document. ‌​"Total impulse (newton-seconds)." ‌​Four words. ‌‌That is all it would have taken.

​​---

The Human Factor

After the failure, journalists and commentators mocked the error. ‌‌"NASA can't do unit conversion!" ​​The jokes wrote themselves. ‌​But the real story is more uncomfortable than a simple math mistake.

‌​Lockheed Martin's engineers used imperial units because that was their institutional standard for propulsion systems. ‌‌JPL used metric because that was NASA's institutional standard for navigation. ​‌Both standards were well-documented within each organization. ​​The gap was not inside either team — it was at the interface between them.

‌​This is a pattern that shows up everywhere in engineering, not just at NASA. ​‌Two competent teams, each following their own conventions, connect their systems at a boundary — and the boundary specification is where ambiguity hides. ‌​Not because anyone is careless, but because the things that are "obvious" inside your team are invisible to the team on the other side of the interface.

​‌The post-failure review board made several recommendations. ‌​The most important one was not about unit conversion. ‌‌It was about verification: every interface specification must be independently validated by both the producing and consuming teams, confirming that they interpret the document the same way. ‌​Not "did you read the spec?" ‌‌but "show me what you think the spec means, and I will show you what I think it means, and we will compare."

​​---

The Cost of Clarity

There is a temptation to dismiss specification precision as pedantry. ‌​"Everyone knows we use metric." ​​"It is obvious what the units are." ‌‌"Adding explicit units to every field would make the document twice as long."

​​The Mars Climate Orbiter is the answer to all of those objections. ‌‌The cost of being explicit was trivial — a few extra words in a document. ‌​The cost of being ambiguous was $327 million and a decade of scientific data that was never collected.

‌​Precision in documentation is not about being thorough for the sake of it. ‌​It is about recognizing that the person reading your document is not you. ​‌They do not share your assumptions. ‌‌They do not know your conventions. ​​They might be in a different building, a different company, a different country, working on a different schedule, with a different set of "obvious" defaults.

​​Write for them. ​‌Not for yourself.

‌​---

Reflection

Think about the technical explanation you wrote in Module 2. ‌​Now think about this:

1. ‌​How many implicit assumptions are in your document? ‌‌Things you know but did not write down because they seemed obvious. ‌​What if the reader does not share your "obvious"? ‌‌Go back and count them. ​‍Every assumption you can name is one you can make explicit.

‌‍2. Lockheed and NASA were both competent, experienced teams. The failure was not stupidity — it was ambiguity in a specification. What specifications or interfaces in your own work have you assumed are clear but never explicitly verified? Have you ever asked the reader "what do you think this means?" and compared their answer to what you intended?

3. The fix was trivially easy — add units to the spec. The cost of not fixing it was $327 million. How do you decide which "trivial" clarifications are worth making in your own documentation? Is there a clarification you have been putting off because it felt unnecessary?

---

Four words could have saved a spacecraft. What four words are missing from your document?
